solution.concept_anchor: Champaner abandonment after Humayun's campaign — political geography and urban continuity
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students may assume the city was abandoned because the Portuguese made it strategically untenable — conflating the Portuguese-Gujarat naval conflict with Humayun's inland campaigns.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a planned city abandoned after a hostile military campaign, with the political centre reverting to an older established city — this maps to Champaner's abandonment after Humayun's 1535 campaign and Gujarat's return to Ahmedabad.
Eliminate option (b): Portuguese involvement pertained to Diu, not Champaner — Champaner was an inland city beyond Portuguese reach.
Eliminate option (c): Champaner's abandonment was caused by Mughal military pressure (Humayun's campaign), not Portuguese activity.

Eliminate option (d): The city was not abandoned due to trade route shifts — it was military-political abandonment following Humayun's campaign; option (a) correctly identifies the principle of military-political geography determining urban continuity.
solution.final_explanation:
Champaner's development and abandonment illustrates how political geography determines urban continuity in medieval India. Mahmud Begada conquered Champaner (1484) and invested enormously in making it a planned Islamic capital. However, when Humayun's campaigns of 1535 demonstrated Gujarat's military vulnerability at Champaner, the political centre reverted to the more defensible and established Ahmedabad.

Applicable principle: A medieval capital's continuity depended on its political-military viability, not merely its architectural investment. When a new capital was exposed to successful enemy action, reverting to an established city was administratively rational — Ahmedabad had deeper infrastructure, population base, and commercial networks.

• Option (a): Correct. The historical principle at work is that Champaner's abandonment after Humayun's 1535 campaign reveals how military exposure could override extensive urban investment. Political geography — the sultanate's defensive needs — determined where the effective capital remained.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Portuguese activity centred on coastal Diu, not inland Champaner — Portuguese pressure played no role in Champaner's abandonment.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Trade route logic does not explain the abandonment — Champaner's commercial role was secondary to its political symbolism as a conquered capital.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The abandonment was abrupt and militarily triggered, not a gradual population shift driven by economic factors.

Value Addition:
• Because Champaner was largely abandoned after 1535, it survived without Mughal-era construction overlaying it — precisely why it qualifies as a UNESCO site.
• Ahmedabad's return as the primary capital post-1535 shows the practical limits of symbolic new-capital building in sultanate politics.
• The Pavagadh hill fort within Champaner contains the Kalika Mata temple — a pre-Islamic structure that survived within the Islamic urban complex.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Gujarat eventually fell to the Mughals under Akbar may confuse Gujarat's experience with Malwa's two-step absorption, selecting Gujarat as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Delhi, Jaunpur, and Gujarat Sultanates were all absorbed directly by Mughal forces — directly from their independent or semi-independent status into the Mughal Empire.
Malwa Sultanate was first absorbed by the Gujarat Sultanate (1531) and only then by the Mughals (1561–62) — it experienced a two-step absorption, making it distinct from the others.
The odd one out is Malwa — the only major sultanate absorbed by another regional sultanate before Mughal conquest → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students may select Gujarat as the odd one out because it absorbed Malwa — confusing the absorber with being absorbed. Gujarat itself was then directly absorbed by the Mughals (1572), making its Mughal absorption direct. Malwa's unique intermediate step — Gujarat Sultanate absorption first (1531), then Mughal absorption (1561–62) — is the distinguishing fact.
solution.final_explanation:
The mode of absorption into the Mughal Empire differed for each regional sultanate. Three of the four options describe sultanates absorbed directly by Mughal forces; one was absorbed by a fellow regional sultanate first.

• Option (a) — Delhi Sultanate: The last Lodi ruler was defeated directly by Babur at Panipat (1526) — direct Mughal absorption.
• Option (b) — Gujarat Sultanate: Absorbed directly by Akbar's Mughal forces in 1572 — a direct Mughal absorption.
• Option (c) — Malwa Sultanate: First absorbed by Gujarat Sultanate under Bahadur Shah (1531), then conquered by Akbar's forces (1561–62). Malwa is the only major sultanate absorbed by another regional sultanate before coming under Mughal rule — this is the odd one out.
• Option (d) — Jaunpur Sultanate: Absorbed into the Lodi Sultanate of Delhi and subsequently into the Mughal Empire — its absorption trajectory was through Delhi, not a regional sultanate peer.

Value Addition:
• Bahadur Shah's 1531 conquest of Malwa is the only instance of one major regional sultanate fully absorbing another in this period.
• Jaunpur fell to Bahlul Lodi of Delhi in 1479, predating the Mughal period.
• The two-step absorption of Malwa (Gujarat then Mughal) is frequently tested as a distinctive historical fact.

statement_analysis.statement: Ahmad Shah I of Gujarat (reigned c. 1411–1442) was a more effective state-builder than Hoshang Shah of Malwa (reigned c. 1405–1435) because Ahmad Shah I successfully founded a new planned capital, subdued internal revolts, and established a durable administrative framework, whereas Hoshang Shah left the Gujarat rivalry unresolved despite a comparable reign length.
statement_analysis.reason: The historical comparison between these two contemporaneous rulers consistently favours Ahmad Shah I as a more effective consolidator — he founded Ahmedabad (1411), suppressed Rajput and tribal resistance, and built durable institutions. Hoshang Shah's long reign (1405–1435) failed to neutralise the Gujarat threat or secure Malwa's external frontiers decisively.

statement_analysis.statement: Hoshang Shah's greatest architectural legacy — his tomb at Mandu — had no influence on later Mughal architecture, as Mughal architects drew exclusively from Persian and Central Asian traditions when designing funerary structures.
statement_analysis.reason: Hoshang Shah's Tomb is specifically documented as having been studied by Shah Jahan's architects before the design of later Mughal marble funerary monuments — it had demonstrable influence on Mughal architectural tradition, directly contradicting the claim of exclusive Persian-Central Asian inspiration.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both rulers well and consider Hoshang Shah's architectural legacy may accept Statement 2 without critically testing the 'exclusively Persian/Central Asian' claim against the documented Shah Jahan connection.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The comparison favouring Ahmad Shah I as more effective state-builder is supported by historical evidence — new capital, internal consolidation, durable framework vs. Hoshang Shah's unresolved Gujarat problem. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: 'Drew exclusively from Persian and Central Asian traditions' is directly contradicted by Shah Jahan's architects studying Hoshang Shah's Tomb — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's trap is the 'exclusively Persian and Central Asian' qualifier. A student who knows Mughal architecture has strong Persian-Central Asian roots may accept this without recalling the specific documented instance of Shah Jahan's architects visiting Hoshang Shah's Tomb. The absolute 'exclusively' makes the otherwise plausible claim false.
solution.final_explanation:
Comparing contemporaneous rulers across different sultanates is a recurring UPSC analytical theme. Hoshang Shah and Ahmad Shah I were near-contemporaries who shaped their respective sultanates in markedly different ways.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Ahmad Shah I's state-building record — founding Ahmedabad (1411), suppressing revolts, and establishing Gujarat's administrative durability — is consistently rated superior to Hoshang Shah's record. Hoshang Shah's long reign produced notable architectural achievements but failed to resolve the core strategic challenge of the Gujarat rivalry.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement's claim that Mughal architects drew 'exclusively' from Persian-Central Asian traditions is historically false. Hoshang Shah's Tomb at Mandu is specifically documented as a structure studied by Shah Jahan's architects before designing major Mughal marble funerary monuments — a clear case of Malwa influencing Mughal architecture.

Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → Option (c).

Value Addition:
• The Taj Mahal's white marble aesthetic is often traced through a chain that includes Hoshang Shah's Tomb as an early Indian marble funerary precedent.
• Ahmad Shah I's 30-year reign (c. 1411–1442) overlapped with Hoshang Shah's, making them true contemporaries and rivals.
• Gujarat's urban planning at Ahmedabad created a model city whose planned layout influenced subsequent urban development in the region.

statement_analysis.statement: In the Muzaffarid dynasty of Gujarat, Mahmud Begada was immediately succeeded by Ahmad Shah I, who oversaw a significant expansion of Gujarat's territorial control.
statement_analysis.reason: Ahmad Shah I preceded Mahmud Begada in the Muzaffarid succession — Ahmad Shah I (c. 1411–1442) was the sultanate's consolidator, while Mahmud Begada (1458–1511) came much later. Mahmud Begada was not succeeded by Ahmad Shah I.

statement_analysis.statement: Bahadur Shah was the last sultan of the Gujarat Sultanate to exercise substantial independent power before the Mughal Empire's expansion effectively ended Gujarat's autonomous political existence.
statement_analysis.reason: Bahadur Shah (1526–1537) was indeed the last powerful sultan of Gujarat; after his death, the sultanate's later rulers were weak and the Mughals progressively subordinated Gujarat until Akbar's formal annexation in 1572.

statement_analysis.statement: The recurrent succession disputes among later Gujarat sultans post-Bahadur Shah structurally mirrored the succession crises that had earlier weakened the Malwa Sultanate after Mahmud Khalji I's death.
statement_analysis.reason: Both sultanates exhibited the same structural weakness: strong founding/peak rulers followed by succession crises and noble factionalism that progressively weakened central authority — a parallel historians have consistently drawn.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Mahmud Begada was Gujarat's most powerful sultan may assume whoever came immediately after him was also a strong ruler involved in expansion, misreading Statement 1 as plausible.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1: Ahmad Shah I (c. 1411–1442) preceded Mahmud Begada (1458–1511) — the statement reverses the chronological sequence entirely, making it factually false. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Test Statement 2: Bahadur Shah as the last powerful sultan before effective Mughal subordination is accurate — Statement 2 is correct.
Test Statement 3: The parallel between post-Mahmud Khalji Malwa and post-Bahadur Shah Gujarat succession crises is a valid historical structural comparison — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct → option (a). Wait — checking options: option (a) = 1 only. Correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 reverses the succession order of two of Gujarat's most important rulers — Ahmad Shah I (founder-consolidator) and Mahmud Begada (peak ruler). Students who know both names but cannot sequence them precisely may accept the reversed order as plausible, especially since both rulers were associated with territorial expansion.
solution.final_explanation:
The Muzaffarid dynasty's succession sequence is a high-precision UPSC question topic. The key sequence runs: Muzaffar Shah I → Ahmad Shah I → (several intermediate rulers) → Mahmud Begada → (further successors) → Bahadur Shah.

• Statement 1 — NOT Correct: This statement reverses the succession order. Ahmad Shah I (c. 1411–1442) was an early and foundational ruler; Mahmud Begada (1458–1511) came much later. Mahmud Begada was succeeded by Muzaffar Shah II, not by Ahmad Shah I (who had lived a generation earlier).
• Statement 2 — Correct: Bahadur Shah (1526–1537) exercised the last phase of substantial independent power. Post-Bahadur Shah successors were largely ineffective, and Akbar's 1572 annexation completed the Mughal takeover.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The structural parallel between Malwa's post-Mahmud Khalji I decline and Gujarat's post-Bahadur Shah trajectory — both characterised by succession disputes and noble factionalism — is historically well-supported.

Value Addition:
• The correct sequence of key Gujarat sultans: Muzaffar Shah I → Ahmad Shah I → Mahmud Begada → Muzaffar Shah II → Bahadur Shah → Mughal annexation (1572).
• Muzaffar Shah II was Mahmud Begada's grandson.
• Gujarat's last sultan Muzaffar Shah III was captured by Akbar and taken to court as a prisoner.

solution.concept_anchor: Gujarat economic depth vs Malwa — seaports, merchants, and trade

statement_analysis.statement: Gujarat's access to the ports of Cambay, Surat, and Broach gave it a revenue base from maritime trade that was structurally unavailable to the landlocked Malwa Sultanate.
statement_analysis.reason: Gujarat's coastal geography providing access to Indian Ocean trade through multiple major ports gave it a sustainable fiscal advantage over Malwa, which lacked any such maritime revenue stream.

statement_analysis.statement: The competition for control over trade routes between Gujarat, Malwa, and Mewar was one of the structural drivers of the triangular rivalry, as all three powers sought to control the commercially lucrative western Indian trade corridors.
statement_analysis.reason: Trade route control was a genuine structural driver of the three-way rivalry — Malwa sat on routes connecting the Deccan and northern India, Gujarat controlled western maritime access, and Mewar controlled key overland corridors in Rajputana.

statement_analysis.statement: The Jain and Bania merchant communities of Gujarat, despite their commercial importance, consistently supported Malwa's sultanate over Gujarat's because Malwa's sultans offered lower tax burdens.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no historical basis for the claim that Jain/Bania merchants systematically preferred Malwa over Gujarat — these communities were integral to Gujarat's commercial ecosystem and maintained pragmatic relations with the Gujarat sultans.

statement_analysis.statement: Gujarat's fiscal superiority over Malwa, derived from port customs and transit trade revenues, helps explain why Gujarat was able to eventually absorb Malwa rather than the reverse.
statement_analysis.reason: Gujarat's stronger economic base (maritime revenues, merchant networks) gave it superior resources for sustained military campaigns, ultimately enabling Bahadur Shah's 1531 conquest of Malwa.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may not flag Statement 3 as incorrect because the claim about 'lower tax burdens' sounds administratively plausible — traders preferring lower tax regimes is intuitive but unsupported by evidence in this specific case.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is clearly correct — Gujarat's port revenue advantage over landlocked Malwa is a structural economic fact.
Statement 2 is correct — trade route competition was a genuine driver of the triangular rivalry.
Statement 3 introduces a fabricated factual claim about Jain/Bania merchants preferring Malwa — no historical evidence supports this. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4 correctly connects Gujarat's economic superiority to its eventual absorption of Malwa — it is correct.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct → option (c) 'Only three'.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a plausible-fabrication technique: the idea that merchants prefer lower-tax regimes is intuitive and sounds historically plausible. But the specific claim — that Jain/Bania merchants systematically favoured Malwa over Gujarat — has no historical basis and inverts what is actually known (these communities were deeply integrated into Gujarat's commercial ecosystem).
solution.final_explanation:
Gujarat's economic foundations explain much of its political durability and eventual dominance over Malwa. The comparison between the two sultanates' economic bases is a recurring analytical theme.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Gujarat's multi-port maritime access (Cambay, Surat, Broach) gave it revenues that landlocked Malwa structurally could not match.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Trade route competition was a genuine structural driver of the Malwa-Gujarat-Mewar triangular rivalry. Each power had a commercial stake in controlling access through contested corridors.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: No historical evidence supports the claim that Jain and Bania merchants systematically favoured Malwa over Gujarat. These communities were integral to Gujarat's commercial ecosystem and maintained working relations with Gujarat's sultans.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Gujarat's superior fiscal resources, derived from maritime revenues, directly enabled its eventual military dominance, culminating in the 1531 absorption of Malwa.

Three statements correct → Option (c).

Value Addition:
• Cambay (Khambhat) was historically one of the world's busiest ports before silting gradually reduced its importance in the 16th–17th centuries.
• The Jain community's financial networks extended from Gujarat into Malwa and Rajputana — their commercial reach transcended sultanate boundaries.
• Malwa's strategic position on the Deccan-North India route gave it transit trade revenue, but this was qualitatively different from Gujarat's maritime customs income.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts are true may select (a) assuming that fighting multiple enemies simultaneously is self-evidently the reason why territorial peak did not lead to regional supremacy — without scrutinising whether 'inconclusive' is the correct characterisation when Mahmud Khalji was the one losing at Sarangpur.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Mahmud Khalji I's reign (1436–1469) represents the maximum territorial extent of the Malwa Sultanate, even though his campaigns were largely inconclusive.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. R states that his victory at Sarangpur allowed consolidation — but Mahmud Khalji I was DEFEATED at Sarangpur by Rana Kumbha in 1437. He did not win at Sarangpur. R is factually incorrect.

The Battle of Sarangpur (1437) is the critical factual test in this question. It was Rana Kumbha's decisive victory over Mahmud Khalji I — not a Khalji victory.

• Assertion (A): Correct. Despite inconclusive military campaigns, Mahmud Khalji I's reign (1436–1469) marked the territorial peak of the Malwa Sultanate — he had ambitions against Mewar, Gujarat, and Delhi simultaneously, and Malwa's geographic reach was at its greatest during his time.
• Reason (R): Incorrect. R claims Mahmud Khalji I 'secured victory at the Battle of Sarangpur' — this is factually false. Rana Kumbha won at Sarangpur and commemorated the victory with the Vijay Stambha at Chittorgarh. Mahmud Khalji I was the loser at Sarangpur.

solution.concept_anchor: Rupmati's Pavilion vs. Rani Rupmati Mosque — two different structures in two sultanates
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who associate 'Rupmati' with Gujarat Sultanate architecture (Rani Rupmati Mosque in Ahmedabad) may confuse the two Rupmati-associated structures and select option (c).
elimination_logic: Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu is associated with Baz Bahadur of Malwa and his queen/consort Rupmati — it belongs to the Malwa Sultanate.
Eliminate option (c): Rani Rupmati Mosque is in Ahmedabad (Gujarat Sultanate) — it is named after a different Rani Rupmati unconnected to Baz Bahadur.
Eliminate option (a): Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu does not belong to Hoshang Shah's period — it dates to the later Malwa sultanate (Baz Bahadur's period).
Option (b) correctly identifies Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu as associated with Baz Bahadur's period and the Malwa Sultanate.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The name 'Rupmati' appears in both the Malwa (Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu — Baz Bahadur's consort) and Gujarat (Rani Rupmati Mosque in Ahmedabad — a different historical figure) architectural traditions. Students who know one Rupmati association but not both will be confused by the name coincidence and may select the wrong sultanate or wrong monument.
solution.final_explanation:
The name 'Rupmati' is associated with two completely different architectural monuments in two different sultanates — a rare coincidence that UPSC has the potential to exploit.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu is not from Hoshang Shah's period — it dates to the reign of Baz Bahadur (1555–1562), the last independent ruler of Malwa.
• Option (b): Correct. Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu is associated with Baz Bahadur's reign and his celebrated romantic connection with the singer Rupmati. It is a Malwa Sultanate structure from the 16th century.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Rani Rupmati Mosque is in Ahmedabad, built during the Gujarat Sultanate period — it is named after a different Rani Rupmati, entirely unrelated to Baz Bahadur or Mandu.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu has nothing to do with the Portuguese period or any Portuguese-associated architecture.

Value Addition:
• Rupmati's Pavilion at Mandu was reportedly positioned so that Rupmati could see the Narmada River from it — a detail embedded in the romance legend.
• The Rani Rupmati Mosque in Ahmedabad (also called Masjid Rani Rupmati) is a Gujarat Sultanate monument named after a queen of the Gujarat sultanate.
• Baz Bahadur's palace at Mandu and Rupmati's Pavilion together constitute the 'lovers' quarter' of Mandu's heritage ensemble.

solution.concept_anchor: Comparative internal and external decline factors — Malwa vs Gujarat

statement_analysis.statement: The absence of a significant naval or maritime commercial base was an internal structural weakness of the Malwa Sultanate that accelerated its decline relative to Gujarat.
statement_analysis.reason: Malwa's landlocked geography meant it could never develop the port revenues and maritime trade networks that gave Gujarat sustained fiscal superiority — this structural disadvantage was a consistent factor in Malwa's relative weakness.

statement_analysis.statement: The rise of the Mughal Empire under Babur and Humayun was the sole external factor driving both sultanates toward decline, as no other external pressure played any meaningful role.
statement_analysis.reason: While Mughal expansion was a decisive external factor, Portuguese pressure on Gujarat's maritime trade was an additional significant external factor — claiming Mughal expansion as the 'sole' factor ignores the Portuguese dimension, which was particularly impactful for Gujarat.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Malwa and Gujarat Sultanates experienced phases where powerful nobles or ministers effectively controlled the sultanate's governance, undermining the sultan's authority and inviting external intervention.
statement_analysis.reason: Medini Rai's dominance in Malwa and noble factionalism in post-Bahadur Shah Gujarat both exemplify this pattern of ministerial/noble power overtaking sultanic authority, which weakened both states and made them vulnerable to external pressures.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know Mughal expansion was the primary driver of both sultanates' decline may accept Statement 2's 'sole factor' claim without accounting for the Portuguese pressure dimension, selecting option (c) (1 and 2 only) instead of option (a).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Malwa's landlocked geography as a structural weakness is accurate and well-supported — Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: 'Sole external factor' ignores Portuguese pressure on Gujarat — this scope-extension makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Statement 3: Noble/minister dominance in both sultanates (Medini Rai in Malwa, post-Bahadur Shah Gujarat factionalism) is accurately described — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's 'sole external factor' qualifier is the scope-extension trap. Students who know Mughal expansion was the dominant driver may not flag the word 'sole' as making the statement false. Portuguese pressure on Gujarat's trade — though secondary to Mughal military pressure — was a genuine additional external factor that the statement's absolutism excludes.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the comparative decline of Malwa and Gujarat requires distinguishing internal structural weaknesses from external pressures, and avoiding absolutist claims about single causation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Malwa's landlocked position denied it the maritime revenues that sustained Gujarat through its periods of internal weakness. This was a permanent structural disadvantage explaining much of the outcome differential between the two sultanates.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 'Sole external factor' is the error. Portuguese disruption of Gujarat's Indian Ocean trade was a significant additional external pressure — particularly impactful because Gujarat's economic strength depended on maritime commerce. The statement's absolutism makes it false.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The pattern of nobles/ministers dominating weak sultans appears in both sultanates. Medini Rai in Malwa and the factional politics of post-Bahadur Shah Gujarat both illustrate this structural parallel.

Value Addition:
• The Portuguese-Mughal dual pressure on Gujarat was unique — no other regional sultanate faced simultaneous maritime and land-based threats from two different imperial powers.
• Medini Rai's dominance in Malwa (early 16th century) is the classic Indian example of a Hindu noble wielding effective power within a Muslim sultanate.
• Structural decline patterns (succession crises, noble dominance, fiscal weakness) are broadly similar across late regional sultanates — making cross-sultanate comparison a productive UPSC analytical theme.

solution.concept_anchor: Malik Ayyaz — governor of Diu under Mahmud Begada
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Diu was associated with the Portuguese may insert a Portuguese commander's name (Francisco de Almeida) into the blank, not recognising that the blank describes Diu's Gujarat administrator, not its Portuguese captor.
elimination_logic: The blank requires a person who: (1) served under Mahmud Begada, (2) was appointed governor of Diu, and (3) had a slave background.
Eliminate option (a): Mir Husain was the Egyptian commander at the Battle of Chaul, not a governor of Diu under Mahmud Begada.
Eliminate option (b): Francisco de Almeida was the Portuguese viceroy who won at Diu — he was never governor of Diu under Gujarat.
Eliminate option (d): Ikhtyar Khan is not a figure associated with Diu's governorship under the Gujarat Sultanate.
Malik Ayyaz served as governor of Diu under Mahmud Begada and rose from slave origins to this administrative position → option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) Francisco de Almeida is the classic entity-swap: students who associate Diu with Portuguese history may insert Almeida's name, not recalling that the blank describes the Gujarat administrator of Diu before the Portuguese period. The blank explicitly says 'under Mahmud Begada' — a qualifier that eliminates all Portuguese commanders.
solution.final_explanation:
Diu was a key naval and commercial hub for the Gujarat Sultanate before it passed into Portuguese control. Its administrator under Mahmud Begada was a remarkable figure in medieval Indian social history.

• Option (a) — Mir Husain: The Egyptian naval commander who co-commanded the allied fleet at the Battle of Chaul (1508) alongside Malik Ayyaz. He was not governor of Diu.
• Option (b) — Francisco de Almeida: The first Portuguese Viceroy of India who won the Battle of Diu (1509). He was never a Gujarat administrator — the entity-swap distractor.
• Option (c) — Malik Ayyaz: Correct. Of Russian/Georgian slave origin, Malik Ayyaz rose through the Gujarat Sultanate's military-administrative hierarchy to become governor of Diu under Mahmud Begada. He developed Diu as a commercial and naval hub and commanded the Gujarat fleet at Chaul (1508).
• Option (d) — Ikhtyar Khan: Not a historically documented figure associated with Diu's governorship under the Gujarat Sultanate.

Value Addition:
• Malik Ayyaz's trajectory from slave to governor parallels the Mamluk tradition in the Delhi Sultanate — social mobility through military service.
• Diu under Malik Ayyaz became a prosperous port connecting Gujarat's inland trade to Indian Ocean networks.
• After Gujarat ceded Diu to Portugal in 1535, the port's character changed fundamentally — it became a Portuguese colonial fortress city.
